mainTopic: Who sets the size of a vowed מצורע offering, and when a person's wealth is measured in ערכין and in offerings
overview: The amud opens by explaining that the משנה's two rules about vowing to pay for a מצורע's offering cover two different cases. A poor sponsor of a poor מצורע may bring the poor offering, but a poor sponsor of a rich מצורע must bring the rich one. A ברייתא learns this from "אם דל הוא". According to רבי, the word "הוא" instead excludes a rich sponsor of a poor מצורע. A new משנה then teaches that in ערכין, being rich either when you vow or when you pay means paying the rich amount, and רבי יהודה says even being rich only in between counts. By contrast, a מצורע's offerings follow only what he has right now. The גמרא brings the פסוקים for these rules, and it learns רבי יהודה's view from "ואם מך הוא": a person counts as poor only if he is poor from start to finish. It defends this reading against the parallel פסוק of the מצורע, which has its own special source, "בטהרתו". It then raises a new challenge from the witness פסוק "והוא עד" and begins quoting a ברייתא about witnesses. The answer to that challenge comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Two rules for two different cases
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's two statements are not repeats. One is about a poor מצורע with a poor sponsor. The other excludes a rich מצורע with a poor sponsor.
steps.simpleTranslation: One rule is about a poor מצורע whose sponsor is also poor. The other rule comes to exclude a rich מצורע whose sponsor is poor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה needs two separate statements about vowing to bring someone else's מצורע offering. Each statement covers a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both the מצורע and the person who vowed are poor, a poor man's offering is enough. If the מצורע is rich, the poor sponsor does not get that leniency and must bring a rich man's offering. This is the second statement's job.

keyTerms.meaning: A person with צרעת, who must bring offerings when he becomes pure
The one who vows for him, meaning the person who promised to pay for his offering
A poor person
A rich person
To exclude, to teach that a case is left out of a rule

steps.confusionAlert: Two different people are involved here: the מצורע, whose offering it is, and the מדיר, who vowed to pay for it. Keep track of which one is rich and which one is poor.

phrases.english: One [rule] is about a poor leper
whose sponsor who vowed for him is poor,
and the other one is to exclude
a rich leper whose sponsor is poor.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲדָא אַמְּצוֹרָע עָנִי וּמַדִּירוֹ עָנִי, וַחֲדָא לְמַעוֹטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers an earlier question, from before this part of the daf, about why the משנה gives two statements.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the statements into two different cases
steps.terutzMaskana: Each statement teaches its own case: poor with poor, and rich with poor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A poor sponsor of a rich מצורע must bring a rich man's offering.

steps.title: Why the second rule was needed
steps.stepSummary: Without the second rule, we might have thought that a poor sponsor could always bring a poor man's offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought: since poor people were included in the lighter offering, they are included in every case. So the משנה teaches us that this is not so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the mistake we would have made without the second statement. It shows why that statement is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah allowed poor people to bring a cheaper offering. One could think this leniency follows the poor sponsor no matter whose offering it is. The משנה teaches that it does not apply when the מצורע himself is rich.

keyTerms.meaning: It would have entered your mind to say, meaning "you might have thought"
They were included in a rule
It teaches us, meaning this is the new lesson

phrases.english: It would have entered your mind to say:
since [poor people] were included [in the cheaper offering],
they are included [in every case, even for a rich leper];
so it teaches us [that this is not so].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the second case from step 1 needed to be taught.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a mistake we would otherwise have made
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because poor people got the cheaper offering, a poor sponsor could always bring it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leniency depends on the מצורע being poor, not on the sponsor being poor.

steps.title: A ברייתא learns this from "אם דל הוא"
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that we might have compared this to ערכין, where the one who vows pays based on his own means. The פסוק "אם דל הוא" teaches otherwise.
steps.simpleTranslation: In ערכין we find that a poor person who valuated a rich person pays a poor person's valuation. One might think that here too it is so. So the פסוק says: "And if he is poor."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports the same idea. It gives the reason we might have made the mistake and the פסוק that rules it out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ערכין, the amount paid depends on the means of the one who vowed. So we might have used the same rule for the מצורע's offering. The word "הוא" ("he") shows that the poor offering depends on the מצורע himself being poor.

keyTerms.meaning: Valuations: vows to give the Temple the fixed Torah value of a person
He valuated, meaning he vowed to give someone's ערך
One might think, a suggestion that the ברייתא is about to reject
The פסוק teaches us
"If he is poor", the פסוק about the poor מצורע's offering

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that offerings and ערכין follow different rules. In ערכין the one who vowed matters. In offerings the owner of the offering matters.

phrases.english: Since we find with regard to valuations
that a poor person who valuated a rich person
gives the valuation of a poor person,
one might think this case too is so;
so the verse says: "And if he is poor."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 14:21. "He" points to the מצורע himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ברייתא source for the rule taught in steps 1 and 2.
steps.raayaObject: A poor sponsor of a rich מצורע brings a rich man's offering.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading "אם דל הוא" as being about the מצורע himself.

steps.title: According to רבי, what does "הוא" exclude?
steps.stepSummary: רבי holds that even in ערכין we follow the obligation of the person being valuated. If so, there was never a reason to make the mistake, so what does "הוא" come to exclude?
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רבי, who says "I say that even in ערכין it is so", he clearly holds that we follow the obligation of the person. If so, no פסוק is needed to exclude this case. So "he" comes to exclude what?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא from the view of רבי. It is setting up the question of what the word "הוא" teaches according to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא needed "הוא" only because ערכין seemed to follow the one who vowed. רבי holds that even ערכין can follow the obligation of the person who was valuated. So the comparison falls away, and the word "הוא" seems to have no job.

keyTerms.meaning: Evidently, it comes out that
We follow the obligation of the person who was valuated or whose offering it is
A פסוק is not needed
To exclude what? meaning what does this word come to leave out?

steps.confusionAlert: רבי does not say that ערכין always follow the rich person. He says that when the obligation already belongs to a person, we follow that person's obligation.

phrases.english: But according to Rabbi, who says:
"I say that even with regard to valuations it is so"
phrases.notes: This is from the משנה: a poor person who takes on a rich person's own valuation pledge pays the rich amount.

phrases.english: evidently he holds:
we follow the obligation of the person,
so a verse is not needed to exclude [this case];
so "he" comes to exclude what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ברייתא's פסוק according to רבי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's use of "אם דל הוא" to exclude a poor sponsor of a rich מצורע
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to רבי, the comparison to ערכין would never lead to the mistake, so the word "הוא" seems to have nothing to exclude.

steps.title: "הוא" excludes a rich sponsor of a poor מצורע
steps.stepSummary: Even according to רבי, the word "הוא" is needed. It teaches that a rich person who vows to pay for a poor מצורע's offerings must bring a rich man's offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word comes to exclude a poor מצורע whose sponsor is rich. You might have thought: since רבי said "we follow the obligation of the person," the rich sponsor could bring the poor man's offering. So the פסוק teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 4: what does "הוא" exclude according to רבי? It excludes the opposite case, a poor מצורע with a rich sponsor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's own rule, that we follow the obligation of the person being valuated, could have led us to say the rich sponsor brings only the poor offering, because the מצורע himself is poor. "אם דל הוא" focuses on the sponsor: only if *he* is poor may he bring the poor offering. So a rich sponsor brings a rich offering, and the word is not extra even for רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: to exclude (the case a word comes to leave out)
the one who vows on his behalf, the sponsor
you might have thought (the mistaken first idea)
the obligation of the person himself (here, the מצורע)
it teaches us (the actual lesson)

steps.whatToRemember: With a poor sponsor, the sponsor's poverty matters only if the מצורע is also poor (step 1). According to רבי, a rich sponsor brings a rich offering even for a poor מצורע. So for רבי, the sponsor's wealth can only make the offering bigger, never smaller.
steps.confusionAlert: Step 1 was about a rich מצורע with a poor sponsor. This step is the reverse: a poor מצורע with a rich sponsor. Keep track of who is rich and who is poor.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבי's rule of following the obligation of the person can be used to make the offering stricter, but not more lenient, when a rich sponsor is involved.

phrases.english: To exclude a poor leper whose vower is rich,
phrases.notes: The word "הוא" in the פסוק "אם דל הוא" comes to exclude this case.

phrases.english: it would enter your mind to say:
since Rabbi said:
"We follow the obligation of the person,"
phrases.notes: Here that means the poor מצורע, so you might think the rich sponsor brings only a poor offering.

phrases.english: so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 4 by giving "הוא" a new case to exclude.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the exclusion to a different case, which is needed precisely because of רבי's view.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Following רבי, a rich sponsor of a poor מצורע might bring only the poor man's offering, since the מצורע is poor.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק teaches that a rich sponsor brings a rich man's offering.

steps.title: משנה: a change in wealth in ערכין means paying the rich amount
steps.stepSummary: If a person who vowed ערכין was rich either when he vowed or when he pays, he pays the rich amount. רבי יהודה adds that even if he was rich only in between, he pays the rich amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If he was poor and became rich, or was rich and became poor, he gives a rich man's valuation. רבי יהודה says: Even if he was poor, became rich, and then became poor again, he gives a rich man's valuation.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It asks at what point we measure a person's wealth when he pays a valuation vow (ערכין).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A poor person who vows ערכין may pay according to what he can afford, and a rich person must pay the full amount. The תנא קמא says being rich at either point, the vow or the payment, makes him pay the full amount. רבי יהודה goes further: being rich at any moment in between also counts, even if he is poor at both ends.

keyTerms.meaning: the full valuation a rich person pays
he became rich
he became poor
he became poor again

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is not arguing about the first two cases. He agrees with them and adds a case where the person was poor both at the vow and at the payment.

phrases.english: MISHNA: If he was poor and became rich,
or rich and became poor,
he gives a rich man's valuation.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
If he was poor, became rich, and again became poor,
he gives a rich man's valuation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new question: the timing of wealth in ערכין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In ערכין, being rich at the vow or at the payment means paying the rich amount. According to רבי יהודה, being rich at any point in between also counts.

steps.title: משנה: for קרבנות only his present situation counts
steps.stepSummary: For the offerings of a מצורע, we look only at what he has now. Expected money, like an inheritance or a ship on its way, does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: But with offerings it is not so. Even if his father died and left him ten thousand, or his ship is at sea and coming to him with tens of thousands, the הקדש has no share in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues and contrasts קרבנות with ערכין. For offerings, wealth is measured only by what he actually has at the time he brings them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ערכין, being rich at an earlier point can obligate a person. For a מצורע's offerings, it is the opposite: he brings according to his present means. Money he is about to receive does not yet make him rich, even a large inheritance or a valuable shipment on the way.

keyTerms.meaning: offerings (here, a מצורע's offerings that depend on wealth)
ten thousand (coins)
the Temple treasury

steps.whatToRemember: ערכין: once rich at a key point, he pays the rich amount. קרבנות: only what he has right now counts.

phrases.english: But with offerings it is not so;
even if his father died
and left him ten thousand,
or his ship is at sea
and is coming to him with tens of thousands,
the Temple treasury has nothing in it.
phrases.notes: He has not received the money yet, so he still brings according to what he has now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה and contrasts קרבנות with ערכין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מצורע's offerings follow his present means only. Expected money does not count.

steps.title: The פסוקים behind both ערכין rules
steps.stepSummary: "Poor then rich" comes from "אשר תשיג יד הנדר": whenever his hand reaches. "Rich then poor" comes from "על פי": what he had when the words left his mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Poor and became rich: from "what the hand of the vower can reach." Rich and became poor: from "according to [by the mouth of] what he can reach."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source in the פסוק for each half of the משנה's ערכין rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "אשר תשיג יד הנדר" means we look at what his hand can reach. If he later became rich, he can now reach the full amount, so he pays it. "על פי" literally means "by the mouth," which points to the moment he spoke the vow. If he was rich then, the rich amount is fixed even if he became poor afterward.

keyTerms.meaning: what the hand can reach (his means)
the one who vowed
according to; literally "by the mouth," pointing to the time of the vow

phrases.english: GEMARA: Poor and became rich:
"what the hand of the vower can reach."
Rich and became poor:
"according to what he can reach."
phrases.notes: "פי" also means "mouth," so we look at the moment he said the vow, when he was rich.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָנִי וְהֶעֱשִׁיר אֲשֶׁר תַּשִּׂיג יַד הַנֹּדֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק source for the two cases of the משנה in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's rule that either earlier or later wealth obligates a rich man's valuation.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ויקרא 27:8: "אשר תשיג יד הנדר" (later wealth) and "על פי" (wealth at the time of the vow).

steps.title: What is the source for רבי יהודה's view?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה's ruling from the משנה and asks for his reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Even if he was poor, became rich, and then became poor again, he pays a rich person's ערך. What is רבי יהודה's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back רבי יהודה's ruling from the משנה so it can ask where he learns it from. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two cases (rich when he vowed, or rich when he pays) were already explained from the פסוקים. רבי יהודה goes further: he says even being rich only in the middle makes you pay like a rich man. The גמרא wants a source for this extra rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Poor, then became rich, then became poor again
The full fixed ערך amount that a rich person pays
What is the reason? (asking for the source or logic)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Even if he was poor and became rich
and then became poor again,
he gives a rich person's valuation.
What is Rabbi Yehuda's reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After deriving the two basic cases in step 8, the גמרא now looks for the source of רבי יהודה's extra case from step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for רבי יהודה's ruling that being rich even only in the middle makes one pay a rich person's ערך.

steps.title: The word הוא means he must stay poor the whole time
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה learns from "ואם מך הוא" that a person counts as poor only if he is poor from beginning to end.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: "But if he is too poor for your valuation." This means he counts as poor only if he stays in his poverty from the beginning until the end.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה reads the word "הוא" ("he") as a limit. Only someone who is poor the entire time gets the poor man's discount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word "הוא" stresses that "he" must be poor the whole time. So if he was rich at any point between the vow and the payment, he loses the poor status. That is why the middle period alone is enough to make him pay the rich amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Poor, lowly (the word the פסוק uses for a poor person in ערכין)
From his beginning until his end, meaning the whole time from vowing until paying

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יהודה, "מך הוא" means a person is treated as poor only if he stays poor the whole time, from the vow until the payment.

phrases.english: The verse says:
"But if he is too poor for your valuation"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 27:8. The key word is "הוא", meaning "he".

phrases.english: only if he remains in his poverty
from his beginning until his end.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: וְאִם מָךְ הוּא מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word "הוא" in "ואם מך הוא" teaches that he counts as poor only if he is poor from start to finish.

steps.title: Then a poor מצורע should also have to stay poor the whole time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the פסוק about a poor מצורע also says "דל הוא", so the same start-to-finish rule should apply there.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, about the מצורע the פסוק says "And if he is poor." So too, he should count as poor only if he stays poor from beginning to end!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. If "הוא" teaches start-to-finish poverty in ערכין, it should teach the same thing for a poor מצורע, where the תורה uses the same word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two פסוקים are built the same way: "מך הוא" for ערכין and "דל הוא" for a מצורע. If the word "הוא" carries this meaning in one place, it should carry it in the other. That would mean a מצורע who was rich at any point during his offerings must bring a rich man's offerings.

keyTerms.meaning: But now that you say so (introducing a problem that follows from the previous answer)
Poor (the word the פסוק uses for a poor מצורע)
So too, the same should be true

phrases.english: But if that is so,
then "And if he is poor"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 14:21, about a poor מצורע. It has the same word "הוא".

phrases.english: should also mean only if he remains in his poverty
from his beginning until his end!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading from step 10 by applying it to a parallel פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's reading of "הוא" as requiring poverty from start to finish.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same word "הוא" appears for a poor מצורע, so the same rule should follow there. The next step shows that this outcome is not accepted.

steps.title: But everyone judges a מצורע by one single moment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that the start-to-finish rule does not apply to a מצורע: a משנה and a ברייתא each judge him by his status at one offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that this is really so, didn't we learn in a משנה: A מצורע who brought his offerings while poor and then became rich, or while rich and then became poor, everything follows the חטאת. These are the words of רבי שמעון. רבי יהודה says: Everything follows the אשם. And a ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: Everything follows the birds!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks the escape of saying the rule really does apply to a מצורע. It brings sources showing that all three תנאים, including רבי יהודה himself, decide based on one point in time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון looks at the time of the חטאת, רבי יהודה at the time of the אשם, and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב at the time of the birds. Each picks a single moment, and none of them requires poverty from start to finish. So רבי יהודה does not read "דל הוא" the way he read "מך הוא", and the question is why.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (heading off a possible answer)
Everything follows, meaning we decide based on that point
Sin offering, one of the מצורע's offerings that changes for rich or poor
Guilt offering of the מצורע, the same for rich and poor
The two birds the מצורע brings at the start of his purification

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי יהודה is contradicting himself about ערכין here. The problem is only that his reading of "הוא" should have carried over to a מצורע, yet he himself rules differently there.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the need to explain why the word "הוא" teaches start-to-finish poverty in ערכין but not for a מצורע.

phrases.english: And if you would say that indeed it is so,
but didn't we learn in a mishna:
A leper who brought his offerings
while poor and then became rich,
or while rich and then became poor:
everything follows the sin offering,
phrases.notes: His status when he brings the חטאת decides whether his עולה is a rich or a poor one.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
everything follows the guilt offering,
and it was taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
everything follows the birds!
phrases.notes: The birds come seven days before the other offerings, at the very start of his purification.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the challenge of step 11 by showing that the rule cannot simply be accepted for a מצורע.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible answer that the start-to-finish rule really does apply to a מצורע.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: All three תנאים, including רבי יהודה, judge a מצורע by his status at one offering. So nobody requires poverty from start to finish for a מצורע, and רבי יהודה's reading of "הוא" seems inconsistent.

steps.title: A special פסוק for the מצורע ties his status to one offering
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that רבי שמעון, רבי יהודה and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב all learn from 'אשר לא תשיג ידו בטהרתו'. Each one ties the מצורע's status to a different offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was already stated about this: רב יהודה said in the name of רב that all three תנאים learned from one פסוק, 'whose hand cannot reach, in his purification.' רבי שמעון holds this means the thing that atones, which is the חטאת. רבי יהודה holds it means the thing that makes him fit, which is the אשם. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds it means the thing that brings his purity, which is the birds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from steps 11-12. The מצורע has his own special פסוק, which says his status depends on one offering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'בטהרתו' (in his purification) tell us to look at his wealth at one key moment of his purification. The three תנאים only argue about which offering that moment is. Since the תורה gave the מצורע a special rule, the start-to-finish rule from 'ואם מך הוא' is not broken by him.

keyTerms.meaning: In his purification; the key word showing that one stage of the process decides his status
The thing that atones (the חטאת)
The thing that makes him fit to enter the מקדש and eat holy food (the אשם)
The thing that brings about his purity (the birds)
The two birds brought at the start of the מצורע's purification

steps.whatToRemember: The מצורע is an exception. A special פסוק ties his rich-or-poor status to one offering, so he does not disprove רבי יהודה's start-to-finish rule for vows.
steps.confusionAlert: The three תנאים do not argue about whether one offering decides. They all agree on that. They only argue about which offering it is.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the מצורע's case is different, so רבי יהודה's reading of 'ואם מך הוא' still stands for someone who vows a ערך.

phrases.english: It was already stated about it:
phrases.notes: 'It' is the dispute in the משנה and ברייתא just quoted in step 12.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
And all three of them expounded one verse:
"Whose hand cannot reach, in his purification."
Rabbi Shimon holds: the item that atones,
and what is it? The sin offering.
And Rabbi Yehuda holds: the item that makes him fit,
and what is it? The guilt offering.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov holds:
that which causes him purity,
and what is it? The birds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge that the מצורע is judged by one offering and not start to finish.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Special פסוק for the case in question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'דל הוא' in the מצורע's פסוק should require start-to-finish poverty, and since it does not, רבי יהודה's reading falls.
steps.terutzMaskana: The מצורע has a special פסוק, 'בטהרתו', which ties his status to one offering. So he is an exception and does not disprove the rule.

steps.title: Then what does the word 'הוא' teach for the מצורע?
steps.stepSummary: If 'בטהרתו' decides the מצורע's status, the גמרא asks what the word 'הוא' in his פסוק is for.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, why do I need the word 'he'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what job the word 'הוא' in 'ואם דל הוא' does, now that it is not teaching start-to-finish for the מצורע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה reads 'הוא' in the ערכין פסוק as 'start to finish'. In the מצורע's פסוק that reading is blocked by 'בטהרתו'. The תורה does not waste words, so 'הוא' must teach something else there.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? Asking what a word is there to teach

phrases.english: But then, why do I need "he"?
phrases.notes: This is the word 'הוא' in 'ואם דל הוא', ויקרא 14:21.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the answer in step 13, which left the word 'הוא' without a job.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the extra word 'הוא' in the מצורע's פסוק teaches.

steps.title: רבי and the רבנן each use 'הוא' for their own rule
steps.stepSummary: The word 'הוא' is used by רבי for his opinion and by the רבנן for theirs. Both are opinions about someone who vows to bring a מצורע's offerings.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רבי, it teaches what he holds. For the רבנן, it teaches what they hold.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'הוא' is already used for an earlier teaching. רבי uses it for his rule and the רבנן use it for theirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי and the רבנן each learned a rule about vowing a מצורע's offerings from 'הוא'. רבי says a rich person who vows a poor מצורע's offering must bring a rich person's offering. The רבנן say a poor person who vows a rich מצורע's offering must bring a rich person's offering. So 'הוא' is not wasted, and it was never needed for start-to-finish.

keyTerms.meaning: As he holds; according to his own opinion stated earlier
The Sages; the majority opinion

phrases.english: According to Rabbi, as he holds,
phrases.notes: 'רבי' alone means רבי יהודה הנשיא, not the רבי יהודה of our משנה.

phrases.english: and according to the Rabbis, as they hold.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְרַבִּי — כִּדְאִית לֵיהּ, וּלְרַבָּנַן — כִּדְאִית לְהוּ
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'הוא' teaches each side's rule about someone who vows a מצורע's offerings: רבי's rule for רבי, and the רבנן's rule for the רבנן.
steps.whatToRemember: The מצורע's 'הוא' is busy with a different teaching, so the מצורע does not disprove רבי יהודה.

steps.title: By the same logic, a witness would need to be fit from start to finish
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's reading again. 'והוא עד' should then mean a witness must be fit from beginning to end.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, 'and he is a witness' should mean: only if he is fit from his beginning until his end!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new challenge to רבי יהודה's way of reading 'הוא' from the פסוק about a witness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה learned 'start to finish' from the word 'הוא'. The witness פסוק also says 'והוא עד'. So the same reading should mean a witness must be fit both when he sees the event and when he testifies. The challenge assumes that this is not the הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: But now, if so; introduces a challenge built on the logic just used
And he is a witness, from the פסוק about a witness who must testify
Fit (here, fit to testify)

phrases.english: But now, if so, "and he is a witness":
only if he is fit
from his beginning until his end!
phrases.notes: Beginning means when he saw the event, and end means when he comes to testify.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the מצורע challenge is answered, the גמרא tests רבי יהודה's reading against another פסוק with 'הוא'.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's reading in step 10 that 'הוא' means 'from beginning to end'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'הוא' always means start to finish, then 'והוא עד' would require a witness to be fit from seeing to testifying. The challenge assumes that is not the rule.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows that a witness does not need to be fit the whole time
steps.stepSummary: Someone might answer that a witness really must be fit from beginning to end. The גמרא rejects this with a ברייתא. It lists cases where a witness who saw something while fit becomes unfit, and then starts a case about someone who becomes a חתן in the middle.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say that this really is the rule for witnesses, isn't it taught in a ברייתא: If someone knew testimony about another person before he became that person's son-in-law, and then he became his son-in-law; or he could hear and then became a deaf-mute; or he could see and then became blind; or he was mentally competent and then became mentally incompetent, he is disqualified. But if he knew testimony about him before he became his son-in-law, and then he became his son-in-law, [the ברייתא continues].
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא expects someone to answer, 'Yes, a witness really must be fit from start to finish.' It starts quoting a ברייתא to show that this is not the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the ברייתא is about a witness who is unfit at the time he testifies, and he is disqualified. That part fits every opinion. The case that begins at the end is the important one. It will show that a witness who is fit at the beginning and at the end can testify even if he was unfit in the middle. If so, 'והוא עד' cannot mean 'fit from start to finish', and the challenge against רבי יהודה's reading gets sharper. The גמרא's answer comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: His son-in-law. A relative, so he may not testify about his father-in-law.
He could hear and speak, and then became a deaf-mute. A deaf-mute may not testify.
His eyes were 'open' (he could see), and then he became blind.
He was of sound mind, and then became mentally incompetent.
Disqualified from testifying.

steps.confusionAlert: The first list (disqualified) does not prove the point. In those cases the witness is unfit when he testifies, and everyone agrees he is disqualified. The proof comes from the case that starts with 'אֲבָל', where he becomes unfit only in the middle.

phrases.english: And if you would say that indeed so,
phrases.notes: He means: yes, a witness really must be fit from beginning to end, as step 16 suggested.

phrases.english: but isn't it taught in a ברייתא:
If someone knew testimony about another person

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁלֹּא נַעֲשָׂה חֲתָנוֹ, וְנַעֲשָׂה חֲתָנוֹ,
phrases.english: before he became his son-in-law, and then he became his son-in-law,
or he could hear and then became a deaf-mute,
or he could see and then became blind,
phrases.notes: Literally 'open', meaning his eyes could see.

phrases.english: or he was of sound mind and then became mentally incompetent
in all these cases he is disqualified.
But if he knew testimony about him

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁלֹּא נַעֲשָׂה חֲתָנוֹ, וְנַעֲשָׂה חֲתָנוֹ,
phrases.english: before he became his son-in-law, and then he became his son-in-law,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָכִי נָמֵי, וְהָא תַּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the challenge of step 16 by closing off the answer 'yes, that really is the law for witnesses'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible reply that a witness truly must be fit from beginning to end, and through it רבי יהודה's reading of 'הוא'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא about witnesses will show that being unfit in the middle does not disqualify. So 'והוא עד' cannot mean 'fit from start to finish', and 'הוא' does not carry that meaning.
